name: Liao Dynasty (Khitan)
summary: A dynasty founded by the Khitan people. It ruled Manchuria, Mongolia and part of north China, and made peace with the Song in 1005.

location.value: Manchuria, the Mongolian Plateau and the Sixteen Prefectures of north China.

terrain.value: Steppe, forest and the northern Chinese plain.
terrain.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

climate.value: Cold continental climate on the steppe and in Manchuria.
climate.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

resources.value: Horses and herds on the steppe, plus the rich farmland of the Sixteen Prefectures.
resources.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

disasters.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

population.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

urbanisation.value: Five capitals for different regions, with Shangjing (Supreme Capital) as the main one.
urbanisation.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

disease.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

migration.value: Chinese farmers and craftsmen were settled in Khitan lands, some as captives.
migration.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

economicBase.value: Herding in the north plus Chinese-style farming in the south, with silk payments from Song.
economicBase.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

tradeRoutes.value: Silk from Song under the Chanyuan Treaty (1005).

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

moneyAndTax.value: Liao bronze coins in the southern districts, with much trade by barter and silk from the Song.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Liao dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

inequality.value: The Khitan imperial Yelü clan and consort Xiao clan ruled; Chinese and other peoples were subjects.
inequality.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

governmentType.value: Absolute monarchy, with separate systems for nomads and Chinese.

succession.value: Hereditary in the Yelü clan, with consorts from the Xiao clan; regents were often powerful.
succession.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

institutions.value: A dual administration: a Northern Chancellery for nomads and a Southern Chancellery run in Chinese style.
institutions.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

stability.value: Long peace with the Song after the Treaty of Chanyuan (1005).
stability.source: Wikipedia: Liao dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between royal princes and the powerful Xiao consort clan.
eliteConflict.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

armyAndTech.value: Armoured Khitan cavalry organised in ordos (camps).
armyAndTech.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

majorWars.value: Wars with the Song ending in the Chanyuan Treaty (1005); wars with Goryeo (993–1019); the Jurchen revolt (1114–1125).
majorWars.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

territoryChange.value: About 2.6 million km² (947), including the Sixteen Prefectures around Beijing.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Liao dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Song China, Goryeo and finally the Jurchen.
alliancesRivals.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

inventions.value: Two Khitan scripts, created to write the Khitan language.
inventions.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

scienceEducation.value: Civil service exams for Chinese subjects; Buddhist printing (the Khitan Tripitaka).
scienceEducation.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

openness.value: Combined Khitan and Chinese culture, with separate systems for each people.
openness.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

religion.source: Wikipedia: Liao dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

languageWriting.value: Khitan, written in the Khitan large script (920) and small script, plus Chinese.
languageWriting.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

artsArchitecture.value: The wooden Yingxian Pagoda (1056) and Buddhist sculpture.
artsArchitecture.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

socialStructure.value: Khitan nobles and herders, Chinese farmers and officials, and other tribal peoples.
socialStructure.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

sharedIdentity.value: Khitan identity kept alive alongside Chinese culture.
sharedIdentity.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

neighbours.value: The Song, Goryeo, Western Xia and the Jurchen.
neighbours.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism flourished, with many pagodas and printed scriptures.
ideasReligions.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

colonisation.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

riseSignals.value: Abaoji united the Khitan tribes and proclaimed himself emperor in 916.

peakPeriod.value: Under Shengzong (982–1031), after the treaty with the Song.
peakPeriod.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Liao dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

outcome.value: Conquered by the Jurchen Jin in 1125; a branch fled west and founded the Western Liao (Qara Khitai).

sources.value: History of Liao. Checked against Wikipedia (“Liao dynasty”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. The founding is dated 907 or 916.

knownFor.label: Yingxian Wooden Pagoda
knownFor.note: The oldest fully wooden pagoda in China.

knownFor.label: Khitan scripts
knownFor.note: Two writing systems made for the Khitan language, still only partly deciphered.

knownFor.label: “Cathay”
knownFor.note: The old European name for China, Cathay, comes from the Khitan.
